query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

measurements: Toughness, grain boundary composition, microstructure, dislocation structure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the results show no correlation between grain boundary decohesion and nanoclustering and brittle behavior, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractDeveloping light yet strong aluminum (Al)-based alloys has been attracting unremitting efforts due to the soaring demand for energy-efficient structural materials. However, this endeavor is impeded by the limited solubility of other lighter components in Al. Here, we propose to surmount this challenge by converting multiple brittle phases into a ductile solid solution in Al-based complex concentrated alloys (CCA) by applying high pressure and temperature. We successfully develop a face-centered cubic single-phase Al-based CCA, Al55Mg35Li5Zn5, with a low density of 2.40 g/cm3 and a high specific yield strength of 344×103 N·m/kg (typically ~ 200×103 N·m/kg in conventional Al-based alloys). Our analysis reveals that formation of the single-phase CCA can be attributed to the decreased difference in atomic size and electronegativity between the solute elements and Al under high pressure, as well as the synergistic high entropy effect caused by high temperature and high pressure. The increase in strength originates mainly from high solid solution and nanoscale chemical fluctuations. Simultaneous improvement of strength and ductility of alloys has been very challenging. Although single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys struggle to meet the high strength requirements of engineering materials, such alloys exhibit high work hardening rates and uniform deformation behavior [,]. These characteristics make high-entropy alloys prone to be an excellent composite matrix. Yang et al. [] reported that the FCC based (CoFeNi)86-Al7Ti7 alloy can be significantly strengthened by the L12 multicomponent intermetallic nanoparticles and exhibit superior strength of 1.5 GPa and ductility as high as 50% in tension at ambient temperature. Liu et al. [] reported that the FCC CoCrFeNiNbx can be significantly strengthened by the Nb-enriched Laves phase with the HCP structure. He et al. [] reported that the addition of Al to the CoCrFeNiMn alloy can form a BCC phase, resulted in a high tensile strength up to 1174 MPa. The above studies show that the formation of high hardness reinforcing particles is an effective way to prepare high performance high entropy composite alloys.

Complex concentrated alloys (CCA) represent a new group of materials, with complex microstructures, comprising of a large number of elements []. CCAs extend the established limits of the high entropy alloys (HEAs) concept by allowing a smaller number of elements in the composition and in various proportions, that can deliver mixed structures containing solid solution and well dispersed intermetallic phases. CCAs generally have higher configurational entropy than conventional alloys and are capable of obtaining complex, disordered compositionally complex solid solution structures. CCAs are distinct from conventional alloys in that they are not based on a single major element and rather include several main elements, which allow a high degree of freedom in alloy compositions and properties. Their properties, such as high temperature resistance, corrosion resistance, workability, and low density, offer a remarkable advantage in the use of CCAs for various extreme conditions applications [,]. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) contain multiple principal (or major) elements, commonly five or more, in equimolar or near-equimolar ratios, differently from conventional alloys. While the configurational entropy of an alloy increases with the increasing number of alloying elements, multiple principal elements of an HEA lead to high entropy of mixing that thus suppresses the formation of intermetallic compounds [,,]. Therefore, stable solid solution phases, such as face-centered cubic (FCC) phase, body-centered cubic (BCC) phase, and hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phase can be obtained [,]. Meanwhile, HEAs have been shown to exhibit outstanding mechanical and chemical properties, such as high strength and hardness [,], exceptional ductility, as well as excellent oxidation and corrosion resistances [], and thus have become potential candidate materials for many challenging industrial applications. The design and application of HEAs require a comprehensive understanding of their properties and underlying deformation mechanisms. decision.trend: Research on high-entropy alloys has been focused on understanding their mechanical properties, such as strength, ductility, and toughness. Earlier studies have shown that these alloys can exhibit excellent strength-ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. However, the mechanisms governing toughness degradation in these alloys are still not well understood. Recent studies have investigated the role of grain boundary decohesion, nanoclustering, and dislocation structure on the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys. The trend suggests that understanding the microstructural evolution and deformation mechanisms is crucial for designing high-entropy alloys with improved toughness.
decision.unsolved: The exact mechanisms governing toughness degradation in high-entropy alloys, particularly the role of grain boundary decohesion, nanoclustering, and dislocation structure, are still not well understood. Additionally, the relationship between microstructural evolution and deformation mechanisms is not fully elucidated.
decision.why: To further understand the mechanisms governing toughness degradation in high-entropy alloys, in-situ or advanced characterization techniques such as atom probe tomography can be employed to investigate the nanoscale microstructure and composition of the alloys. This can provide valuable insights into the role of grain boundary decohesion, nanoclustering, and dislocation structure on the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys.
